title: How Much Will Your Organization Change
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article explores how leaders systematically misjudge the pace of organizational change, tending to overestimate what will shift in the near term while underestimating the scope of change over a five-to-ten-year horizon. Drawing on a Murakami quote about emerging changed from a storm and a Herb Kelleher line about strategic planning, the piece argues that change accumulates through small daily actions rather than single dramatic decisions, making it deceptively slow until it suddenly appears fast. The practical takeaway is a caution against long-range strategic plans, which the author claims routinely age into irrelevance.
points: Leaders reliably overestimate how much will change in one to two years and underestimate how much will change in five to ten.
Change accumulates through a constant stream of small actions rather than single big decisions, which is why its pace is so easy to misread.
Strategic plans stretching beyond a one-to-two-year horizon tend to require revision so often that they become effectively worthless.
Looking back at five-year strategic plans typically reveals how laughably wrong their predictions turned out to be.
quotes: To compete and achieve in an ever-changing marketplace, leaders and organizations have to do things they have never done before. They either change or disappear.
When you come out of the storm, you won’t be the same person who walked in. That’s what the storm is all about.
That’s how change works — its magic. Change is slow until it’s fast.
Take a look at five-year strategic plans in retrospect and you’ll see they are generally laughable in their ambition, prediction, and focus.
